A bulging eye, new double vision, eye-socket pressure, or unexplained vision changes can be orbital tumor symptoms, but they can also result from thyroid eye disease, inflammation, infection, vascular disorders, and other conditions. An exam can help identify the cause without assuming a tumor is responsible.

What Are Common Orbital Tumor Symptoms?

The orbit is the bony socket containing the eye, muscles, nerves, blood vessels, fat, and other tissues. Because these structures share a confined space, an orbital mass can affect nearby eye function.

A 2026 NCBI clinical review of benign orbital tumors notes that possible signs and symptoms include:

  • a bulging eye, also called proptosis
  • double vision or restricted eye movement
  • eye or orbital pain
  • decreased or blurred vision
  • eyelid changes, including drooping

Some orbital tumors cause few or no symptoms at first. Symptoms vary with the mass’s location and effect on nearby structures.

Does a Bulging Eye Always Mean There Is a Tumor?

No. Proptosis and other orbital symptoms can have non-tumor causes. The same NCBI review includes thyroid eye disease, inflammatory disorders, and infections among conditions that can resemble an orbital mass.

Appearance alone can’t confirm the cause; changes in eye position, movement, or vision need an exam to determine what is happening inside the orbit.

What Happens During an Orbital Tumor Evaluation?

An orbital tumor evaluation may include checks of vision, pupils, eye movement, and how far the eye projects forward. Imaging often plays an important role when a mass is suspected.

The Oculofacial Society’s orbital tumor guidance explains that CT or MRI may be used to locate and evaluate a tumor, and some cases require biopsy. Some benign tumors can be observed, so finding a mass doesn’t automatically mean surgery is needed.

When Is Orbital Tumor Surgery Considered?

Treatment depends on the diagnosis, symptoms, location, and effect on surrounding structures. Tumors affecting vision, eye movement, or eye position may be considered for surgery, while some lesions can be monitored or treated another way.

AestheticEye provides evaluation and orbital tumor surgery in southwest Ohio. Depending on the diagnosis and location, care may also involve other specialists.

FAQ About Orbital Tumor Symptoms

Are all orbital tumors cancerous?
No. Orbital tumors can be benign or malignant, and evaluation is needed to determine the type of mass.

Can an orbital tumor cause double vision?
Yes. A mass can affect or restrict eye movement, which may lead to double vision.

Does an orbital tumor always require surgery?
No. Treatment depends on the diagnosis, symptoms, location, and effect on nearby structures.
